ko-pha-ngan.intro: Ko Pha Ngan's great tree is a Yang Na in the village of Ban Nok, in the south of the island, a few kilometres from the Thong Sala pier. Thailand's Ministry of Culture listed it as a heritage tree of the land in 2018 and recorded a girth of 14.64 metres, a height of 53.5 metres and an age of about 400 years. It stands beside the public road, free to see, with small spirit houses at its foot.
ko-pha-ngan.meta_description: Ko Pha Ngan's giant Yang Na in Ban Nok: about 400 years old and 53.5 metres tall by Thailand's heritage tree register, free beside the road.
ko-pha-ngan.question_meta: The oldest tree on Ko Pha Ngan is the giant Yang Na of Ban Nok, about 400 years old by Thailand's heritage tree register.
ko-pha-ngan.question_answer: The oldest tree we know of on Ko Pha Ngan is the giant Yang Na in Ban Nok, in the south of the island. Thailand's Ministry of Culture put it at about 400 years when it listed the tree as a heritage tree of the land in 2018. The age is an estimate, not a count of rings.
ko-pha-ngan.question_context: The tree is a Yang Na, Dipterocarpus alatus, a tall tropical tree of the dipterocarp family. The Ministry of Culture's 2018 list of heritage trees of the land records a girth of 14.64 metres and a height of 53.5 metres, and says the tree won first prize in a 1999 Kasetsart University contest for the largest Yang Na. The register calls it the biggest Yang Na in Thailand; we have not found an independent national survey to confirm that. Other Yang Na grow around the village, and the register notes that bees nest in this one's crown. The tree stands beside the public road in Ban Nok, about 300 metres past Wat Pho in the Ban Tai area, roughly four to five kilometres from Thong Sala pier, where the ferries from Ko Samui and Surat Thani come in. It is free to see at any hour. Villagers treat it as sacred, so the spirit houses and cloth at its foot are offerings, and the low fence keeps the ground around it clear.

faq.q: Is the giant tree on Ko Pha Ngan free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands beside the public road in Ban Nok, about 300 metres past Wat Pho, with no gate or fee. The road is narrow, so daylight is the better time.

faq.q: How big is the Yang Na of Ban Nok?
faq.a: Thailand's heritage tree register records a girth of 14.64 metres and a height of 53.5 metres. The girth may include the swelling at the base.

faq.q: How do I get there from Thong Sala?
faq.a: It is about four to five kilometres from Thong Sala pier, by songthaew towards Ban Tai, taxi or hired motorbike. We have not checked times or fares.

kantang.intro: Kantang, a town south-west of Trang, keeps the spot where Thailand's first rubber tree was planted, by the Ministry of Culture's account in 1901. A roadside memorial with plaques stands beside a living rubber tree on Trangkhaphum Road at the entrance to the town. Visitors report the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so this is the place where Thai rubber began rather than a tree from that year.
kantang.meta_description: Thailand's first rubber tree in Kantang, Trang: a roadside memorial and living tree where rubber planting began around 1900, free to visit.
kantang.question_meta: Kantang's best-known tree is Thailand's first rubber tree, planted around 1900 by the official account, on Trangkhaphum Road.
kantang.question_answer: The tree Kantang is known for is Thailand's first rubber tree, on Trangkhaphum Road at the entrance to the town. Thailand's Ministry of Culture says the first seedling was planted here in 1901; a tourist guide says 1899. The trunk standing now may have regrown from the original, so its own age is unknown.
kantang.question_context: The Ministry of Culture listed the tree as a heritage tree of the land in 2017. Its account says the governor of Trang, Phraya Ratsadanupradit, wanted rubber seedlings from Malaya and was refused, so an official, Phra Sathonsathanphitak, brought them from Indonesia and planted the first at his residence in Kantang in 1901. The governor then trained officials and spread planting through the province, which is why he is remembered as the father of Thai rubber. A tourist guide tells it differently, with seedlings from Malaya planted in 1899 by the governor himself. Both accounts put the first tree on this spot. The register measured a tree about 20 metres tall and two metres round, in the care of Kantang municipality. Visitors have reported that the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so we give it no age. The memorial is a free roadside stop with plaques, open at any hour, at the entrance to Kantang, south-west of the city of Trang.

faq.q: Is Thailand's first rubber tree still alive?
faq.a: A living rubber tree stands at the memorial, and the Ministry of Culture listed it in 2017. Visitors report the trunk has been cut back and regrown more than once, so it may have grown again from the original rather than being the 1901 trunk itself.

faq.q: When was the first rubber tree planted in Thailand?
faq.a: The Ministry of Culture says 1901, from seedlings brought from Indonesia; a tourist guide says 1899, from Malaya. Both place it here in Kantang.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to visit?
faq.a: No. It is a roadside memorial with plaques on Trangkhaphum Road, open at any hour.

krabi.intro: Krabi's heritage tree is a rain tree in the grounds of Wat Thammawut Saranaram, once Wat Bo Phlo, at Ban Khlong Siat in Nuea Khlong district, outside Krabi town. Thailand's Ministry of Culture listed it in 2018 and measured a trunk 8.12 metres round and about 25 metres tall. The abbot says it came up by itself before the temple was founded, more than about 200 years ago. We have not yet confirmed the tree's exact spot, so treat the pin as a pointer.
krabi.meta_description: Krabi's heritage rain tree at Wat Thammawut Saranaram, Nuea Khlong: 8.12 metres round and more than about 200 years old by the abbot's account.
krabi.question_meta: Krabi's oldest listed tree is the rain tree of Wat Thammawut Saranaram in Nuea Khlong, more than about 200 years old.
krabi.question_answer: The oldest tree Thailand's heritage register lists in Krabi is the rain tree of Wat Thammawut Saranaram, in Nuea Khlong district. The abbot puts it at more than about 200 years, reasoning from the history of the temple, which the tree is said to be older than. That is an estimate, not a count of rings.
krabi.question_context: The Ministry of Culture listed the tree in 2018 as a heritage tree of the land, from the abbot's account. He told the ministry that the tree grew up by itself and was already standing before the temple was founded, so its year is unknown. The temple, once called Wat Bo Phlo, is counted locally as the second temple founded in Krabi province, and the register reasons from that to an age of more than about 200 years. It measured a trunk 8.12 metres round and a height of about 25 metres, and notes that the present crown grew out again from the original trunk. The temple stands at Ban Khlong Siat in Pakasai subdistrict, Nuea Khlong district, outside Krabi town. We have not been able to confirm exactly where: the pin on our map is the register's own point, on the main road in Nuea Khlong, and may be a few kilometres off. Ask locally for Wat Thammawut Saranaram or for Wat Bo Phlo. Entry to the temple grounds is free; it is a working temple, so dress as for any wat.

faq.q: Where is Krabi's heritage rain tree?
faq.a: In the grounds of Wat Thammawut Saranaram, once called Wat Bo Phlo, at Ban Khlong Siat in Pakasai subdistrict, Nuea Khlong district. Our pin is the register's point and has not been checked on the ground, so ask locally for the temple.

faq.q: How big is the rain tree of Wat Thammawut Saranaram?
faq.a: Thailand's heritage tree register measured a trunk 8.12 metres round and a height of about 25 metres when it listed the tree in 2018.

faq.q: Can you visit it for free?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in the grounds of a working temple with no entry charge. Dress modestly, as at any Thai temple.

takua-pa.intro: Takua Pa, north of Khao Lak in Phang Nga, has Khlong Sang Ne, a short canal where old figs meet overhead from both banks and the community paddles visitors through the tunnel. People call it the Little Amazon. Thailand's Ministry of Culture listed the canal's fig in 2017 as a heritage tree of the land, at more than 200 years; a 2023 PPTV report says more than 100. The trip takes about an hour and a half and is booked ahead for the tide.
takua-pa.meta_description: The Little Amazon at Khlong Sang Ne, Takua Pa: a tunnel of heritage figs over a canal, seen on a community paddle-boat trip north of Khao Lak.
takua-pa.question_meta: Takua Pa's heritage tree is the fig tunnel of Khlong Sang Ne, the Little Amazon, more than 100 years old by PPTV and 200 by the register.
takua-pa.question_answer: The best-known old trees near Takua Pa are the figs of Khlong Sang Ne, which arch over the canal to form a tunnel known as the Little Amazon. Thailand's Ministry of Culture listed them in 2017 at more than 200 years, from the community's account, while a 2023 PPTV report says more than 100. Read the age as a range.
takua-pa.question_context: Khlong Sang Ne is a short canal in Bang Nai Si, Takua Pa district, Phang Nga province, north of Khao Lak. Old figs lean in from both banks and meet overhead, their roots hanging into the water among other waterside trees, and the Ministry of Culture listed the canal's fig in 2017 as a heritage tree of the land. Its record, written from the Khlong Sang Ne community's account, describes blunt-leaved weeping figs more than 200 years old, the largest over two metres round and more than 20 metres tall, in a place where fresh and salt water mix and hornbills and snakes live. A 2023 report by the broadcaster PPTV gave the tunnel more than 100 years. The figs are seen from the water: the community runs paddle-boat trips with no motors, about an hour and a half long, and PPTV advises booking ahead so the trip can be timed to the tide. Takua Pa is a little over an hour's drive from Phuket. Our pin is the register's point beside the canal, not a confirmed boat launch, so ask the community tourism group where to meet when you book.

faq.q: How do you see the Little Amazon at Khlong Sang Ne?
faq.a: From a paddle boat on a trip run by the Khlong Sang Ne community, about an hour and a half long. Book ahead so the trip can be timed to the tide, and ask where the boats leave from.

faq.q: How old are the figs of Khlong Sang Ne?
faq.a: Thailand's heritage tree register says more than 200 years, from the community's account; a 2023 PPTV report says more than 100. Read it as a range.

faq.q: How far is Khlong Sang Ne from Phuket?
faq.a: A little over an hour's drive, by PPTV's account. It is in Bang Nai Si, Takua Pa district, north of Khao Lak.
